edits.why_correct: Failure of eyelid closure in a lower motor neurone facial palsy exposes the cornea, which can dry out, ulcerate and scar. Eye care is therefore part of initial management: regular lubricating drops during the day, and ointment with gentle taping of the lid at night. Pain, redness or visual change should prompt same-day ophthalmology review. Source: RCEM Learning, Acute facial palsy management; consistent with NICE CKS, Bell's palsy.

edits.why_correct: Long-standing chronic ear disease can spread to the adjacent temporal lobe or cerebellum, forming an abscess. The combination of headache, fever, vomiting, drowsiness and a focal cerebellar sign points to a space-occupying intracranial infection, which needs urgent imaging and neurosurgical and microbiology input. Source: standard teaching on intracranial complications of chronic suppurative otitis media (see NICE CKS, Otitis media - chronic suppurative).

edits.why_correct: A positive Romberg test, where balance worsens when vision is removed, indicates loss of proprioceptive (or vestibular) input, because the eyes normally compensate for the missing sensory information. With reduced vibration and joint position sense in a diabetic patient, the picture fits a sensory ataxia from peripheral neuropathy. Source: standard clinical neurology examination teaching (Oxford Handbook of Clinical Medicine).

Clinically fine, but NG217 does not define ictal phases (writer's own note), so the citation is misleading.

edits.why_correct: The postictal phase is the recovery period after a seizure, in which drowsiness, confusion, headache and sometimes transient focal weakness are common. It follows the ictal phase (the seizure itself) and gradually resolves. Source: standard epilepsy terminology (ILAE seizure classification).

issues: Sound terminology item; RCP stroke guideline cite generic but acceptable.

CKS meralgia paraesthetica could not be verified (CKS 403; searches found no CKS/NHS page), so 'verified against CKS' is unsupported. Clinical content (LFCN entrapment, obesity/belts, conservative management) is standard and supported by Cochrane/reviews. Citation replaced; management wording softened. No live meralgia item.

edits.why_correct: Isolated burning and numbness over the anterolateral thigh with normal power and reflexes is typical of meralgia paraesthetica, entrapment of the lateral femoral cutaneous nerve, a purely sensory nerve. Obesity, weight gain, pregnancy and tight belts or clothing are recognised triggers. Management is conservative: reassurance, removing the trigger and weight loss, with neuropathic pain treatment or specialist referral if symptoms persist. Source: Cochrane Review, Treatment for meralgia paraesthetica; standard clinical neurology teaching.

issues: Content sound. NG128 states last known to be well (incl. wake-up strokes) in thrombectomy recs 1.4.5-1.4.7; citation made specific (NG128 amended since 2022).

edits.why_correct: Eligibility for thrombolysis and thrombectomy depends on how long ago the stroke started. When onset was not witnessed, as with a wake-up stroke, the clock starts from the time the person was last known to be well, and treatment decisions are then guided by that time and by imaging. Source: NICE NG128, Stroke and transient ischaemic attack in over 16s, recommendations 1.4.5-1.4.7 (last known to be well, including wake-up strokes).

Clinical content correct. NICE CKS has no myasthenia gravis topic (could not verify); citation replaced. No live non-ocular generalised MG recognition item (NEU022/BX070/PAQ16007/NEU055 ocular).

edits.why_correct: Weakness that builds with repeated or sustained activity, including bulbar fatigue, and recovers with rest is the hallmark of myasthenia gravis, an antibody-mediated disorder of the neuromuscular junction. Reflexes and sensation are typically preserved and creatine kinase is normal. Diagnosis is supported by acetylcholine receptor antibodies, with further tests if these are negative. Source: Association of British Neurologists, UK guidance on the management of myasthenia gravis; NHS, Myasthenia gravis.

issues: Verified against NG71 recs 1.5.13-1.5.20 (evaluate and treat triggers; do not treat if well tolerated; reduce triggering drugs with specialist advice; quetiapine/clozapine; no olanzapine; other antipsychotics worsen motor features). Citation year simplified to the 2017 recommendations.

edits.why_correct: NICE advises a general medical evaluation for anyone with Parkinson's hallucinations and treatment of any trigger found, such as infection. If the hallucinations are well tolerated by the patient and family, they should not be treated. Treatment is considered only if they become distressing, and then involves specialist-guided dose reduction and quetiapine or clozapine. Source: NICE NG71, Parkinson's disease in adults, recommendations 1.5.13-1.5.20.

issues: Diagnosis sound. CKS page unverifiable (403) so the 2024 date was unsupported; removed. Near live PAQ14929/PAN7492/NEU010 but those are migraine with aura or a feature question; accepted.

edits.why_correct: Recurrent unilateral throbbing headaches lasting hours, with nausea and sensitivity to light, and complete recovery between attacks, fit migraine without aura. The normal examination and absence of red flags make a secondary cause unlikely. Source: NICE CKS, Migraine; NICE CG150, Headaches in over 12s.

issues: Verified NG127 1.7.2 and 1.10.2 (immediate referral for rapidly progressive symmetrical weakness/numbness; assess bulbar and respiratory function). Distinct from live NEU003/NEU102/NEU051 (inpatient management) and BX426 (diagnosis).
Anatomy correct, but NG232 does not mention anosmia; citation overstated. Replaced.

edits.why_correct: Anosmia after head trauma is typically caused by shearing of the delicate olfactory nerve fibres as they pass through the cribriform plate of the ethmoid bone, and it can occur even when CT is normal. Taste seems reduced because flavour depends heavily on smell, so a bland taste with normal facial and visual function points to olfactory nerve injury. Source: standard clinical neuroanatomy (olfactory nerve, cranial nerve I) and head injury teaching.

issues: Dystonia/cervical dystonia with sensory trick is correct; distractor definitions accurate. No live duplicate (NEU079/P072 are acute drug dystonia treatment).
Clinically correct (L3-L4 quadriceps, knee jerk). Citation mislabelled MRC scale (grades power, not root levels). Learning point adjacent to live BX643 (femoral nerve) but tests root level; accepted.

edits.why_correct: Straightening the knee depends on the quadriceps, which is supplied by the femoral nerve from the L3 and L4 roots, and the knee jerk is mediated by the same roots. Weak knee extension with a reduced knee jerk and normal ankle findings therefore localises to L3-L4. Source: standard myotome and reflex levels, UK undergraduate clinical neurology teaching.

issues: Todd paresis correct. NG217 does not mention Todd paresis (writer admitted); citation replaced.

edits.why_correct: Temporary focal weakness lasting minutes to hours after a seizure is Todd's paresis (postictal paralysis), thought to reflect neuronal exhaustion in the area that seized. It resolves spontaneously, and a normal scan with a clear temporal relationship to a witnessed seizure supports it. Source: standard clinical neurology teaching on postictal (Todd) paresis; Epilepsy Society.

issues: Content correct. CKS MS page unverifiable (403) so the claim of CKS review date is unsupported; citation made general. No live Lhermitte item.

edits.why_correct: Lhermitte sign is a brief electric-shock sensation running down the spine and limbs on neck flexion. It reflects irritability of demyelinated dorsal column pathways in the cervical cord and is classically described in multiple sclerosis, which fits her earlier optic neuritis. It can also occur with other cervical cord disease. Source: standard clinical neurology teaching; MS Trust, Lhermitte sign.

issues: Wernicke localisation correct; RCP stroke guideline does not give the localisation, citation overstated. Replaced. Not a duplicate of BX169 (type) or PAQ15259 (Broca location).

edits.why_correct: Fluent but meaningless speech with poor comprehension is receptive (Wernicke) aphasia. Wernicke area lies in the posterior part of the superior temporal gyrus of the language-dominant hemisphere, which is the left in almost all right-handed people. Because the motor cortex is spared, limb strength is often normal. Source: standard clinical neuroanatomy of language areas.

issues: Vertebrobasilar TIA localisation correct; NG128 refer-immediately/24h TIA assessment accurate. Differs from live BX919/NEU047 (acute posterior stroke) and PAN5163 (MCA).

Clinically sound; key moved correctly. why_wrong D called functional disorder a 'diagnosis of exclusion' (outdated; it is made on positive signs). Closest live items PAQ16373 (dropped cup, acute stroke) and PAQ16275/BX627 (laterality) share the stroke theme but hemianopia plus hemiparesis is a distinct angle; accepted.

edits.why_wrong: A. A detached retina affects one eye only and does not cause limb weakness. C. Optic neuritis affects one eye with pain on movement and causes no limb weakness or field loss in both eyes. D. Functional disorder is diagnosed on positive clinical signs, and a hemianopia with weakness fits a structural lesion. E. Migraine aura develops gradually over minutes, is positive in character and does not usually cause hemiparesis.

issues: Content correct. Citation was from memory and CKS page unverifiable (CKS blocked), so replaced with NICE NG127 (covers narcolepsy/cataplexy referral) and ICSD. Close to live PAQ15793 (laughter-triggered knee buckling -> narcolepsy) but asks a different question (what the episode is vs seizure/syncope/TIA); accepted, caller may judge.

edits.why_correct: These are episodes of cataplexy, a sudden, brief loss of muscle tone triggered by strong emotion such as laughter, and it is characteristic of narcolepsy type 1. Awareness is retained throughout and recovery is immediate, which separates it from seizures and syncope. Source: NICE NG127, Suspected neurological conditions: recognition and referral, 2019; International Classification of Sleep Disorders.

Clinical content correct. Year on CKS Sciatica citation unverified (CKS blocked); removed. Overlap with BX983/BX1058 (which root) is the reverse direction (movement from foot drop); accepted.

edits.why_correct: This is foot drop, a weakness of ankle dorsiflexion produced by tibialis anterior and the other anterior compartment muscles. The toes drag during the swing phase, so the patient lifts the knee high (a steppage gait) and the foot slaps down. A common cause is an L5 radiculopathy, as here, or a common fibular nerve lesion. New foot drop needs a prompt neurological assessment to find the level of the lesion. Source: NICE CKS, Sciatica (lumbar radiculopathy).

issues: Clinical content correct (recurrent motor branch; thenar wasting/weakness is a CKS surgical-referral trigger). CKS year unverified; removed.

edits.why_correct: In long-standing carpal tunnel syndrome, compression of the median nerve at the wrist can damage its recurrent motor branch, which supplies the thenar muscles that abduct, flex and oppose the thumb. Wasting of the thenar eminence with weak opposition indicates advanced compression. Thenar wasting or weakness is a reason to refer for consideration of surgical decompression rather than continuing conservative treatment. Source: NICE CKS, Carpal tunnel syndrome.
edits.notes: Re-angled the bare 'which muscle group' recall into a clinical picture with wasting, adding the referral implication (thenar wasting/weakness as a surgical referral trigger per CKS). Distractors changed to varied muscle groups with different nerve supplies; source's 'triceps' and 'deltoid' replaced. Near live items (RHE002, BX069, BX1015) test diagnosis/nerve/splinting, not motor involvement. CKS page could not be fetched by writer or checker; content is standard teaching.

Clinically sound (dysautonomia in GBS). CKS year unverified; removed.

edits.why_correct: Guillain-Barre syndrome can affect autonomic fibres, causing labile blood pressure, arrhythmias and heart rate swings that may need intensive care monitoring. Once sepsis, drugs and volume problems are excluded, dysautonomia is the likely explanation. Source: NICE CKS, Guillain-Barre syndrome.

issues: Clinically sound. Citation 'NHS, Transient global amnesia' not verifiable (NHS page returns 404) and 'ABN, Practical Neurology review' vague; replaced with Bartsch and Deuschl, Lancet Neurol 2010.

edits.why_correct: Transient global amnesia is a sudden loss of the ability to lay down new memories, with repeated questioning and preserved personal identity, alertness and other neurological function. It is often triggered by emotional stress or exertion and settles within hours without treatment. A normal neurological examination and no other deficit make a seizure, TIA or delirium less likely. Source: Bartsch T, Deuschl G. Transient global amnesia: functional anatomy and clinical implications. Lancet Neurology, 2010.
edits.notes: New vignette with a typical emotional trigger. Diagnosis clinical, benign, self-limiting; atypical features should prompt investigation. No NICE guideline exists for TGA; citation replaced by checker with Bartsch and Deuschl 2010.

edits.why_correct: Myasthenia gravis affects the neuromuscular junction of the extraocular and levator muscles but does not involve the smooth muscle that controls the pupil, so pupils stay normal. A dilated, poorly reactive pupil implies parasympathetic involvement from a compressive or other third nerve lesion and should prompt urgent assessment and imaging. Source: Standard UK neurology and neuro-ophthalmology teaching (not covered by a NICE guideline).
edits.notes: Re-angled the 'pupils usually spared' recall item as a discriminating-finding question. No guideline source; checker replaced the Oxford Handbook citation with a generic teaching statement. Related live items NEU022, NEU085.
